newsitem.title: UK: New UK government launches defence review.
newsitem.headline: New UK government launches defence review.

text.p: The new Labour government, eager to define Britain's role in the post-Cold War era, on Wednesday launched a strategic defence review of its armed forces.
Defence Minister George Robertson insisted the main aim was not to cut costs. "It is not Treasury-driven," he told reporters.
Britain's defence spending has been cut by 30 percent in the past five years as a peace dividend heralding the end of the Cold War against the Soviet empire.
Robertson sought cross-party consensus for the six-month review by the defence and foreign ministries and said defence should not be allowed to become a political football.
The Labour Party, landslide winner of the May 1 election, has ditched old pledges to leave the European Union, scrap Britain's nuclear weapons and abandon the arms race.
Robertson adopted a very different tone, pledging: "We will maintain strong conventional forces and our national nuclear deterrent."
He is to stage two seminars and set up a panel of experts to review Britain's defence role and consult the opposition parties on which direction to take.
Robertson, eager to adopt the U.S. model of cross-party consultation, said: "I think it's right we should take defence out of the political arena and stop considering it to be a political football."
Britain has 17,000 troops in Northern Ireland where Irish republican guerrillas are battling for Irish unity. It also has 5,000 troops in Bosnia with NATO peacekeeping forces.
"New security challenges confront us, including the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, aggressive nationalism and international terrorism," Robertson said.
Pessed on whether Britain might contemplate cutting its 23,000-strong presence in Germany, he would not be drawn.
"It is much too early to say in advance what our position is going to be on a whole series of issues, including our troops and equipment held in Germany at the present time."
Britain is the world's second biggest arms dealer in the world after the United States with annual exports topping 5 billion pounds ($8 billion).

Robertson pledged no change. "Making sure this country has got a good and competitive defence industry is something this government has a considerable interest in and will make a priority," he told reporters.
"There isn't going to be a moratorium on procurement decisions but they will clearly be taken in the light of the ongoing discussions inside the review," he said.
